description: UK relationships with the UN, NATO, the Commonwealth, the Council of Europe and the WTO.
content_html:
Why Does the UK Join International Organisations?

No country can solve the world’s biggest problems alone. Climate change, nuclear weapons, terrorism, and global trade all require nations to work together. International organisations provide the forums, rules, and resources that make this cooperation possible. The United Kingdom is a member of several major bodies, each with a different focus and set of responsibilities.

Key Fact

The UK’s five main international organisations are the United Nations (UN), the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO), the Commonwealth, the Council of Europe, and the World Trade Organisation (WTO). After leaving the European Union in January 2020, the UK is no longer an EU member but still participates in some associated arrangements.

The United Nations

The United Nations (UN) was founded in 1945 after the Second World War, with the goal of preventing future conflicts. It has 193 member states and works through a number of key bodies. The Security Council handles threats to international peace and can authorise military action or sanctions. The General Assembly allows every member state one vote on major issues. Specialised agencies include the World Health Organisation (WHO), UNICEF (children), UNESCO (education and culture), and the World Food Programme.

The UK is one of five permanent members of the Security Council, alongside the United States, China, France and Russia. This status gives the UK a veto over Security Council resolutions. Supporters argue this reflects the UK’s global responsibilities and gives it disproportionate influence in maintaining world peace. Critics argue that the veto prevents timely action when permanent members have conflicting interests, as has been seen in several conflicts since 1945.

When a conflict or natural disaster creates a humanitarian crisis, non-governmental organisations (NGOs) such as Oxfam, Save the Children and Médecins Sans Frontières work alongside UN agencies to provide food, shelter, medical care and protection. The UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) coordinates responses for displaced people, while the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) manages overall international relief efforts.

The UK contributes to UN operations through both financial contributions and, at times, military personnel deployed on UN peacekeeping missions. These missions operate under strict rules of engagement: UN peacekeepers are authorised to use force only in self-defence or to protect civilians, and they must operate with the consent of the host nation where possible. The effectiveness of peacekeeping is a matter of ongoing debate — supporters point to reduced conflict in places such as Cyprus and the Democratic Republic of Congo; critics note cases where peacekeepers were unable to prevent atrocities, as in Rwanda in 1994.

NATO

The North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) was founded in 1949 during the Cold War, primarily to provide a collective defence against the Soviet Union. The UK is a founding member. Article 5 of the NATO treaty states that an armed attack against one member is considered an attack against all — this principle of collective defence is the alliance’s cornerstone.

Supporters of NATO argue that the alliance has prevented major war in Europe since 1949 and that collective defence deters aggression from hostile powers. Critics question whether the cost of maintaining NATO commitments — member states are expected to spend at least 2% of GDP on defence — is proportionate to the benefits, and whether the alliance’s eastward expansion has contributed to international tensions. These are contested political arguments, and reasonable people hold different views.

The Commonwealth

The Commonwealth is a voluntary association of 56 countries, home to about 2.5 billion people. Most members were once part of the British Empire, though some have joined without a colonial connection to Britain. The Commonwealth promotes shared values including democracy, human rights, and the rule of law, and supports development through technical assistance and trade links.

Unlike the UN or NATO, the Commonwealth has no military or enforcement powers. Critics argue this limits its effectiveness. Supporters argue that its voluntary, cooperative nature makes it a positive model for international relations, particularly in helping smaller and developing member states access expertise and economic partnerships they could not obtain independently.

Key Fact

The Council of Europe was founded in 1949 and is entirely separate from the European Union. It produced the European Convention on Human Rights (1950), which the UK helped draft. The Council of Europe now has 46 member states. The UK remains a full member, and the Human Rights Act 1998 incorporated the Convention into domestic UK law. This means Brexit did not remove ECHR rights from UK citizens.

The Council of Europe and Human Rights

A common misconception is that the European Convention on Human Rights is an EU institution. It is not. The Council of Europe is a completely separate body from the EU, and the UK’s membership of the Council of Europe was not affected by Brexit. The European Court of Human Rights, which sits in Strasbourg, enforces the Convention and can rule that a member state has violated a person’s rights.

This is one of the most common misconceptions in GCSE Citizenship. The European Union and the Council of Europe are different organisations. When the UK left the EU in January 2020 it left the EU’s institutions (the European Parliament, the European Court of Justice, the single market, the customs union). It did not leave the Council of Europe, and the European Convention on Human Rights — enforced by the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg — still applies in full. The Human Rights Act 1998, which incorporated ECHR rights into UK domestic law, also remains in force. There is a separate ongoing political debate in the UK about whether to reform or replace the Human Rights Act, but at the time of writing the Act is still law.

The World Trade Organisation

The World Trade Organisation (WTO) was established in 1995 to set the rules governing international trade. It provides a framework for negotiations between countries about tariffs, subsidies and market access, and it operates a dispute-resolution process when countries believe another nation is trading unfairly. The UK’s departure from the EU’s single market and customs union in 2020 means the UK now trades with the EU on terms agreed in the UK–EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA) rather than as an EU member. The UK also trades with non-EU countries either via bilateral trade agreements or under WTO rules.

Supporters of the UK’s departure from the EU argue that it gives the UK freedom to negotiate independent trade deals with countries around the world, including with fast-growing economies in Asia and the Americas. Critics argue that the UK’s largest trading partner remains the EU, and that trading outside EU membership involves more administrative complexity and costs for businesses. Both of these are contested political positions and students should present them as such.
exam_tip_html: For extended-response questions about international organisations, the most common error is treating them all as the same type of body. Examiners want you to distinguish between them: the UN is universal and focuses on peace and human rights; NATO is a military alliance; the Commonwealth is a voluntary cultural and development network; the Council of Europe enforces human rights via the ECHR; the WTO governs trade. For a 12-mark Evaluate question, pick ONE organisation, present the case for UK membership (security, influence, cooperation) AND the case against or for reform (cost, sovereignty, effectiveness), then reach a substantiated judgement — “On balance, UK membership of X is beneficial because… although critics raise valid concerns about…”. Also avoid the ECHR/EU confusion: stating that Brexit removed ECHR protections is a factual error and will cost marks.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The UK belongs to five major international organisations — the UN, NATO, the Commonwealth, the Council of Europe and the WTO — each serving a different purpose ranging from peacekeeping to trade governance.
  • Brexit in January 2020 took the UK out of the European Union but did not affect membership of NATO, the Commonwealth, the Council of Europe or the WTO. The European Convention on Human Rights still applies to the UK through the Human Rights Act 1998.
  • Every international organisation involves trade-offs: membership brings cooperation, influence and resources, but also obligations, costs and shared sovereignty — arguments for and against must both be presented when evaluating their value.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following bodies produced the European Convention on Human Rights?
A) The European Union
B) The United Nations
C) The Council of Europe
D) NATO
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for C) The Council of Europe.

practice_questions.text: Identify two international organisations the UK belongs to other than the European Union.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of any two distinct organisations from: the United Nations (UN); NATO; the Commonwealth; the Council of Europe; the World Trade Organisation (WTO). Maximum 2 marks. Near-duplicate answers (e.g. naming the same body twice under different descriptions) score once only.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which the United Nations works to maintain international peace and security.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per way described. Credit two developed points from the following or equivalent:
• The Security Council can authorise military action or impose sanctions on states that threaten peace (1 for the point; 2 for development, e.g. naming the five permanent members or explaining what sanctions involve).
• The UN deploys peacekeeping forces (blue helmets) to conflict zones to protect civilians and maintain ceasefires (1 for the point; 2 for development).
• UN agencies such as the World Food Programme and UNHCR coordinate humanitarian aid during crises (1 for the point; 2 for development noting how NGOs work alongside).
• The General Assembly provides a forum where all 193 member states can vote on major global issues (1 for the point; 2 for development).

Do not credit evaluation or judgement here — description only is required.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

A fictional news report states: 'A 2024 poll of 1,800 UK adults conducted by an independent research organisation found that 61% believed the UK should remain a member of NATO, 22% said the UK should withdraw, and 17% were unsure. Those in favour most often cited security and collective defence; those against most often cited the cost of meeting the 2% GDP spending commitment.'

What does the source tell us about public opinion on UK membership of NATO? Use the source and your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks:
1 mark for identifying what the source shows (a majority, 61%, support UK NATO membership).
1 mark for interpreting the significance of the data (a clear majority but not unanimous; over one in five oppose).
1 mark for using own knowledge to contextualise (e.g. NATO's collective defence principle, Article 5, the 2% GDP target, or the UK's founding membership status).
1 mark for a substantiated judgement that combines source and own knowledge (e.g. noting that the poll reflects genuine division — cost and sovereignty concerns are real policy debates, not just fringe views — while the overall direction of public opinion appears to support continued membership).

Do not credit answers that only summarise the poll without interpreting it or drawing on own knowledge.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the benefits and drawbacks of the UK's membership of the United Nations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): Sustained two-sided analysis with named examples on each side (e.g. UK permanent Security Council veto as a source of global influence; 2019 UN report criticising UK poverty levels as a limitation). Weighs evidence and reaches a substantiated judgement about which side of the argument is stronger.

Secure (5–6 marks): Both benefits and drawbacks are identified and developed. At least one named real-world example (a specific UN body, an example of UN action, or a named outcome). Some weighing of the two sides but judgement may be limited.

Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points on one or both sides but development is limited OR argument is one-sided. May list several benefits or drawbacks without developing any in depth.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic relevant points, little or no real-world reference, largely descriptive.

Benefits to credit: permanent Security Council seat and veto gives the UK disproportionate international influence; access to collective peacekeeping and humanitarian resources; platform to set global agenda on issues such as climate, health and disarmament; strengthens diplomatic relationships.

Drawbacks to credit: veto system can lead to deadlock; cost of UN financial contributions; UK positions can be outvoted in the General Assembly; UN peacekeeping operations have not always prevented atrocities.

practice_questions.text:
"The UK's membership of international organisations does more harm than good because it limits the country's sovereignty and independence."

Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should consider arguments that support this view, arguments that challenge it, and reach a substantiated conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): Full two-sided argument with named examples on each side. Engages directly with the concept of sovereignty. Reaches a substantiated conclusion that goes beyond 'it depends' — e.g. argues that the loss of sovereignty is outweighed by the security and influence gained, or vice versa, with supporting reasoning. May distinguish between different organisations (UN, NATO, Council of Europe, WTO) to show that the trade-off differs by body.

Secure (7–9 marks): Both sides developed with at least one named real-world example. Concludes, but the judgement may be partially substantiated.

Developing (4–6 marks): Relevant arguments on both sides but limited development OR one-sided. Some real-world reference.

Emerging (1–3 marks): Basic points; little real-world example; largely descriptive.

Arguments supporting the statement: international organisations require member states to follow shared rules, potentially overriding national preference (e.g. WTO rules constrain unilateral trade policy; ECHR judgements have required UK law to change on issues such as prisoner voting rights); membership costs money that could be spent domestically; the Brexit referendum reflected public concern about sovereignty.

Arguments challenging the statement: sovereignty is exercised, not surrendered, through international cooperation — the UK voluntarily joins and can leave organisations; collective action delivers outcomes no single state could achieve (e.g. NATO deterrence, WHO pandemic coordination); the UK gains global influence disproportionate to its size through its UN Security Council seat; trade via the WTO framework benefits the UK economy. The Commonwealth and Council of Europe are explicitly voluntary with no enforcement over domestic policy beyond human rights.

Conclusion to credit: a judgement that weighs the sovereignty cost against the cooperation benefit with specific reference to at least one named organisation.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is a permanent member of the UN Security Council?
What does Article 5 of the NATO treaty state?
options: All members must spend 2% of GDP on defence
Members must share intelligence with each other
An attack on one member is an attack on all
Members cannot go to war without UN approval

knowledge_checks.q: The European Convention on Human Rights was produced by the _____, not the European Union.
The _____ was founded in 1995 to set the rules governing international trade and resolve trade disputes between countries.
Match each international organisation to its main purpose:
right: Collective military defence alliance founded in 1949
Voluntary association of 56 states promoting democracy and development
Sets rules for global trade and resolves trade disputes

flashcard_questions.q: In what year was the United Nations founded, and why?
flashcard_questions.a: 1945, after World War Two, to prevent future conflicts and maintain international peace.

flashcard_questions.q: How many permanent members does the UN Security Council have?
What power does a UN Security Council permanent member hold?
flashcard_questions.a: A veto — the power to block any substantive resolution.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Article 5 of the NATO treaty?
flashcard_questions.a: An attack on one NATO member is considered an attack on all members.

flashcard_questions.q: How many member states does the Commonwealth have?
What organisation produced the European Convention on Human Rights?
flashcard_questions.a: The Council of Europe (not the EU).

flashcard_questions.q: Did Brexit remove ECHR protections from UK citizens?
flashcard_questions.a: No. The UK remains in the Council of Europe. The Human Rights Act 1998 is still in force.
Sets rules for international trade and resolves trade disputes between countries.

flashcard_questions.q: When did the UK leave the European Union?
Name one UN specialised agency and its focus.
flashcard_questions.a: UNICEF focuses on children's welfare and rights worldwide.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the role of an NGO in a humanitarian crisis?
flashcard_questions.a: To deliver aid such as food, shelter and medical care independently of governments.

glossary_terms.definition: Worldwide bodies that bring together member states to cooperate on shared issues such as security, trade or human rights.
An international organisation founded in 1945 with 193 member states, aiming to maintain peace, promote human rights and coordinate responses to global challenges.
The power held by each of the five permanent Security Council members to block any substantive resolution.
Non-governmental organisations that operate independently of governments to deliver humanitarian aid and advocate for those in need.
A military alliance of 32 member states in North America and Europe, founded in 1949, committed to collective defence under the principle that an attack on one is an attack on all.
A voluntary association of 56 member states, mostly former territories of the British Empire, cooperating on democracy, development and the rule of law.
An international body founded in 1995 that sets the rules for global trade between nations and resolves trade disputes.

items.title: In Our Time — On Liberty
items.description: Mill's liberal philosophy underpins the values of international cooperation and human rights law — the intellectual foundation for organisations like the Council of Europe and the UN.

items.title: Newscast — BBC Sounds
items.description: BBC's daily podcast — episodes regularly cover UN Security Council actions, NATO, Commonwealth and trade disputes, providing real-world context for this lesson.

items.title: We Can't Even Agree on How Many Countries Exist — CGP Grey
items.description: An engaging exploration of how states, territories and international recognition work — great context for understanding why international organisations like the UN have 193 members.

items.title: What Does It Mean to Be a Refugee? — TED-Ed
items.description: Explains how the 1951 UN Refugee Convention works in practice — directly relevant to the UN's role in protecting human rights globally.

items.title: He Named Me Malala (2015)
items.description: Malala's advocacy at the UN shows international organisations in action — her 2013 speech to the UN Youth Assembly is one of the most watched examples of global civic campaigning.

items.title: Brexit: The Uncivil War (2019)
items.description: A dramatisation of the 2016 Brexit referendum — examines why the UK's relationship with international institutions became such a divisive political question.

items.title: The Commonwealth — Our Work
items.description: The official Commonwealth site explains the organisation's structure, member countries and how it promotes democracy and development — directly covers the lesson content.
